title: Containment of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata
formal: Is quantitative containment decidable for pairs of finitely ambiguous probabilistic automata? Given two rational probabilistic automata \(A,B\) over the same finite alphabet, each promised to admit its own uniform finite bound on the number of positive accepting runs per word, decide whether \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\). Neither automaton is required to be unambiguous, and the sought algorithm is unconditional.
why: Pointwise probability comparison is a basic refinement test for stochastic finite-state descriptions. Resolving this case would determine whether a constant bound on accepting multiplicity suffices to make exact comparison effective, just below a model in which linear growth of that multiplicity already permits undecidability.
status_note: The 2018 conference paper and 2021 journal conclusion explicitly leave this exact containment problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 found no decision or undecidability theorem for both finitely ambiguous inputs. Source proofs were not independently verified and the status is not an exhaustive certification.

progress.text: The ICALP paper explicitly leaves the two-finitely-ambiguous containment problem open.
The journal version retains the open problem, distinguishes the directional partial results, and gives undecidability for linearly ambiguous automata.

importance.reason: Exact containment for bounded-ambiguity stochastic automata is a basic decidability frontier, separating fixed finite accepting multiplicity from a linearly ambiguous model with undecidable comparison. Its arithmetic obstruction reaches beyond one construction or parameter improvement.
importance.basis: Individual source and problem review; editorial significance judgment, not a certification of present-day openness.

sentences: Two probabilistic automata assign acceptance probabilities to every finite input word.
Each machine has a fixed finite bound on its positive accepting runs, but either bound can be greater than one.
The question asks for an unconditional terminating test of whether the first probability never exceeds the second.
Existing results with an unambiguous side do not settle the general case, and allowing linearly growing ambiguity already gives undecidability.
The benchmark requires a Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof for exact comparison without a gap promise.

definitions: A probabilistic automaton is \(A=(\Sigma,Q,\delta,\iota,F)\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), nonnegative rational initial weights \(\iota(q)\) satisfying \(\sum_q\iota(q)\leq1\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \(\delta(q,a,p)\) satisfying \(\sum_p\delta(q,a,p)\leq1\) for each state \(q\) and letter \(a\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.

For \(w=a_1\cdots a_m\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_m\in F\) and \(\iota(q_0)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\). Its weight is this product. Let \(p_A(w)\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \(p_A(\varepsilon)=\sum_{q\in F}\iota(q)\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.

Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \(K\geq0\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \(K\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.

Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.

Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every pair under the two finite-ambiguity promises, or a Lean-checked proof that this promise problem is undecidable. The proof must be unconditional. Restricting one side to unambiguous automata, approximating probabilities, or assuming a numerical gap does not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: The primary paper leaves containment open when both input automata have uniformly bounded accepting ambiguity. The individual bounds may differ and need not be fixed across instances.

The journal version maintains that question. It proves unconditional decidability when the right side is unambiguous and conditional decidability, using Schanuel’s conjecture, when only the left side is unambiguous. Neither result covers arbitrary finite ambiguity on both sides.

The same journal paper proves undecidability when ambiguity may grow linearly with word length. A finite word-independent bound is therefore a substantive proposed decidability boundary. The narrower conjecture-removal target is TCS-0133.

statement_review.notes: Recovered the exact pointwise probability-containment problem with independent finite-ambiguity promises on both sides. Specified rational subdistributions, positive accepting runs, uniform bounds over all finite words including epsilon, and an unconditional total decider. Kept both-sided finite ambiguity distinct from the one-unambiguous conditional theorem and from approximation or gap emptiness. Individually assessed the former midpoint importance.
